chapter_title: Understanding Decentralized Applications (DApps) and Web3 Interaction

screens.title: Decentralized Applications and Web3 Interaction
screens.subtitle: How frontends, wallets, libraries, and smart contracts form a working DApp

narration.text: In this chapter we will learn what makes an application decentralized and how browser code talks to smart contracts. A DApp replaces a centralized backend with smart contracts that hold state and enforce rules on a public ledger. You will see why this matters: DApps can be censorship resistant and give users direct control of assets, but they also introduce new constraints like gas costs and immutable logic. We'll build a mental map connecting four pieces you already know: a standard web frontend, deployed smart contracts, a Web3 provider or node endpoint, and the user's wallet which signs transactions. Practically, you will follow a simple lab pattern: connect a wallet, read a value from a deployed AdvancedStorage contract, and submit a transaction to update it. As you listen, consider how reading data differs from writing data: reads are free calls; writes need a signature, gas, and confirmation. A common pitfall is assuming a contract address or ABI is interchangeable—mistakes there cause failed interactions. By the end you'll be able to explain DApp architecture, use Ethers. js to create a contract instance, and reason about when a wallet must sign. Ask yourself: which part of this stack do you control as a frontend developer, and which part requires coordination with a deployed contract?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A DApp pairs a familiar web UI with smart contracts and a Web3 provider; wallets bridge the user to the blockchain by signing transactions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to concrete developer skills you must practice. First, you will be able to define a Decentralized Application and clearly state how it differs from a traditional web app. That means naming the decentralization properties: no single backend operator, public verifiability, and autonomous execution. Second, you will describe a typical DApp architecture—frontend UI, smart contract backend, and Web3 provider—and explain the responsibilities of each component. Third, you will explain how Web3 libraries like Web3. js or Ethers. js act as bridges: they abstract JSON-RPC calls so your JavaScript can query state and send transactions. Fourth, you will understand how user wallets manage private keys and sign transactions, and why this signing step is essential for any state-changing operation. Each objective includes a compact mnemonic or mental model and a verification milestone so you can test your competency. Practically, this chapter also prepares you for a lab where you connect MetaMask, read a value from a deployed AdvancedStorage contract, and send a signed transaction to update it. Keep in mind a common misconception: decentralization does not remove complexity—it shifts trust to code and the network. Will you be ready to manage both user experience and decentralized constraints?

screens.subtitle: Practical outcomes and common debugging skills

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and troubleshooting. You will learn to identify the contract address and ABI as essential sources of truth for interactions. In the lab you will replace placeholder values with your deployed AdvancedStorage address and its ABI to instantiate a contract instance. You will also learn to distinguish read-only calls from transactions that need signatures and gas; this distinction helps you avoid unnecessary prompts or failed transactions. screens.title: What is a Decentralized Application (DApp)?
screens.subtitle: Definition, properties, and a contrast with traditional web apps

narration.text: A Decentralized Application, or DApp, is an application whose backend logic and persistent state live on a decentralized peer-to-peer network such as a blockchain. The defining properties are simple: the business rules are encoded in smart contracts, state is stored on-chain where it is publicly verifiable, and no single party can arbitrarily change the rules. Concretely, this contrasts with a traditional web app where servers and databases are controlled by one organization. For example, a centralized notes app may store user data in a private database and allow administrators to remove entries. A similar DApp would store entries on-chain under contract rules, and only transactions with valid signatures could alter state. A common misconception is to assume decentralization removes the need for careful design; in reality, decentralization shifts trust from operators to code and immutable deployments, so bugs become harder to patch. Another misconception is thinking everything must be on-chain: good DApp design often keeps large or private data off-chain while storing authoritative references on-chain. Takeaway: DApps trade centralized control for transparency and user ownership, and that trade requires deliberate choices about what lives on-chain and how users sign operations.

keyIdea.title: DApp definition
keyIdea.text: DApps run logic and store authoritative state on a decentralized network, providing censorship resistance and verifiability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › What is a DApp?
Decentralized Application (DApp)
An app where backend logic and state rely on a blockchain rather than a central server.
Definition
Logic in smart contracts, state on-chain, users transact with signed messages.
Properties
  • Transparency: public verifiability of transactions.
  • Censorship resistance: no single operator can take it down.
  • Immutability: deployed code is permanent unless upgrade patterns are used.
Key Takeaway

DApps shift trust to code and the network; design trade-offs decide what belongs on-chain.

Analogy: Shared ledger vs private notebook
A centralized app is like a private notebook held by one person; a DApp stores entries in a shared ledger everyone can audit. This gives transparency but requires careful controls since entries are permanent.
Concrete example
A voting DApp uses contracts to record votes immutably, while a centralized voting site stores votes in a private database.
Common misconception
Decentralization does not guarantee usability; wallets and gas introduce UX friction.
Why this matters
Understanding the DApp concept helps you decide what to implement on-chain, how users will interact, and how to mitigate immutable bugs through design patterns.

screens.title: DApp Architecture: Frontend, Smart Contracts, Provider
screens.subtitle: Roles and interactions among components

narration.text: A clear architecture prevents confusion when building a DApp. At a high level, there are three cooperating layers. The frontend is standard web code—H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript frameworks like React—that renders the user interface and prepares requests. The smart contract backend replaces a centralized server and database; it defines rules and persistent state on the blockchain. The Web3 provider sits between them: it offers an RPC endpoint and, in many browser contexts, a wallet-injected provider that forwards JSON-RPC calls. For example, your frontend may prepare a call to read a public state variable. The provider sends a read call to a node; no user signature is required. For a state change, the frontend asks the provider for a signer, the wallet prompts the user to approve gas and cost, signs the transaction, and sends it to the network. A common misconception is to think the frontend can unilaterally change on-chain state; it cannot—state changes require a signed transaction. When designing a DApp, identify which data can remain off-chain to save gas and which values must be authoritative on-chain. Consider also latency: on-chain confirmations take time, so design UI flows that surface pending state and confirmation results to users. What steps will you add to your UI to make transaction latency transparent to an end user?

keyIdea.title: Architecture summary
keyIdea.text: Frontend prepares requests; provider connects to a node; smart contracts enforce rules and hold authoritative state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › DApp Architecture
Component Roles
Understand who does what and why each layer matters.
Frontend (UI)
Build with familiar web frameworks. Handles user input, displays pending transactions and confirmations, and prepares contract calls.
Smart Contract Backend
Holds authoritative state and logic on-chain. Only transactions signed by accounts can change this state.
Web3 Provider
Connects to a node. Wallets like MetaMask inject providers that can request signatures from users.
Interaction sequence
A typical write sequence: frontend prepares transaction → provider requests signature via wallet → user approves and signs → signed transaction is broadcast → network mines and confirms. Reads skip the signature step and are executed as node calls.
Concrete example
Clicking "Set Data" triggers a signer request; MetaMask prompts approval and shows gas details; after confirmation, the frontend polls for the updated value.
Misconception
The frontend cannot bypass network rules or sign transactions without the user's wallet and approval.
Key Takeaway

Design UI flows that show pending state, confirm transactions, and handle retries or user cancellations gracefully.

screens.title: Smart Contract Backend
screens.subtitle: State, business logic, and immutable deployments

narration.text: Smart contracts are the authoritative backend for a DApp. They encapsulate business logic and store state on the blockchain. When you deploy a contract, its code and initial state become part of the chain; calls to its public functions either read state or create transactions that alter state. A concrete example is an AdvancedStorage contract with a getData view function and a setData function that stores a new value and emits an event. Reading getData requires only a node call and costs no gas; calling setData creates a transaction that the user must sign and pay gas for. A typical developer misconception is assuming contract code can be changed later like a server-side patch — in most deployments, contracts are immutable. That means you must design upgradeability patterns or plan for migrations ahead of time. Another practical point is event design: emitting structured events on state changes allows frontends to listen for updates without polling continuously. Finally, think about on-chain data granularity: storing only essential authoritative values on-chain while keeping large blobs off-chain saves gas and preserves performance. As you design contracts, ask: which functions are view-only and which must be transactions, and how will the UI communicate this to users?

keyIdea.title: Contract role
keyIdea.text: Smart contracts store authoritative state and implement rules; they are immutable and require signed transactions to change state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Smart Contract Backend
What the smart contract provides
Authoritative logic, persistent state, and events that frontends can observe.
View vs Transaction
Views read state without gas; transactions change state and require signatures and gas.
Events
Emit events for important state changes so frontends can react without constant polling.
Immutability
Once deployed, contracts are fixed unless upgradeability patterns are planned in advance.
Design prompt

Choose which data must be on-chain for trust and which can be stored off-chain to save gas.

Concrete example: AdvancedStorage
Functions: getData() view returns a uint256; setData(uint256) updates state and emits DataChanged. The frontend reads getData without signatures and calls setData using a signer and a transaction.
Misconception
Treating smart contracts like replaceable server code leads to fragile upgrades; plan migrations or proxies if upgrades are needed.
Key Takeaway

Contracts are the single source of truth. Design functions and events to support predictable frontend behavior and debugging.

screens.title: Web3 Providers and Libraries (Ethers.js / Web3.js)
screens.subtitle: How libraries abstract JSON-RPC and enable contract calls

narration.text: Web3 providers and JavaScript libraries are the glue that lets frontend code communicate with Ethereum nodes and contracts. A provider is an RPC interface: it accepts JSON-RPC method calls, like requests to get a block number or call a contract method. Libraries like Web3. js and Ethers. js wrap that complexity and provide friendly APIs: they create provider objects, construct contract instances from an ABI and address, and expose methods for read-only calls and transactions. For example, with Ethers. js you create a BrowserProvider or Web3Provider, request accounts, then get a signer object representing the user's account. From the signer you create a contract instance bound to that account so state-changing calls automatically include the correct signature. A common misconception is that Ethers. js and Web3. js do the signing themselves; they only coordinate signing through the provider and the wallet. Another practical detail: some providers are read-only endpoints like Infura; they cannot sign transactions, so you still need a wallet or private key to sign writes. When building, be explicit about which provider you use for reads and which provider-signer pair you use for writes. Ask yourself: how will you surface provider errors or network mismatches to users in the UI?

keyIdea.title: Providers & libraries
keyIdea.text: Libraries abstract RPC; providers connect to nodes; signers represent accounts and enable state-changing transactions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Web3 Providers & Libraries
Provider, Signer, Contract
Ethers.js and Web3.js give a consistent developer model to interact with contracts.
Provider
Connects to a node and performs read and broadcast operations. Examples: MetaMask-injected provider, Infura, Alchemy.
Signer
Represents a user's account capable of signing transactions after user approval.
Contract instance
Created with address and ABI; methods map to contract functions for reads and writes.
Practical note
A read-only provider can fetch state but cannot sign transactions. Signing requires a wallet or private key bound to a signer object. Always test both read and write flows with the same network and correct provider configuration.
Concrete example
Using Ethers.js: create a BrowserProvider, request accounts, getSigner, then new Contract(address, ABI, signer) to perform setData and getData operations in the demo.
Key Takeaway

Be explicit about provider capabilities: which endpoints can sign, and which are read-only, and surface provider mismatches to users.

screens.title: Ethers.js Example: Connect, Read, Write
screens.subtitle: A guided read-through of the interaction pattern

narration.text: Let's walk through the typical Ethers. js interaction pattern used in the lab. First, detect a provider in the browser. If MetaMask is present, you create a BrowserProvider or Web3Provider and send an eth_requestAccounts call to request the user's accounts. That returns control to the wallet for approval. Second, obtain a signer from the provider; the signer represents the user's account and can sign transactions. Third, instantiate a contract object by providing the deployed contract address and its ABI. Reading a public variable involves calling the view function on the contract instance; this is a node call and requires no signature. Writing requires calling a state-changing function on the contract instance through the signer: the wallet will prompt the user with gas estimations and a confirm dialog. A concrete example in the lab is calling getData to display the current value and then calling setData with a new number, waiting for the transaction to be mined before re-reading the value. A common mistake is pasting the ABI incorrectly or leaving a placeholder address; this causes method resolution errors or failed calls. Closing question: after you call setData, how will your UI show a pending transaction versus a confirmed state?

keyIdea.title: Interaction pattern
keyIdea.text: Detect provider → request accounts → get signer → instantiate contract → read or send transaction, then wait for confirmation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Ethers.js Example
Code walkthrough
A minimal sequence used in the demo and lab.
Steps
  1. Detect window.ethereum and create a provider.
  2. Request accounts with eth_requestAccounts.
  3. Get signer and instantiate contract with address and ABI.
  4. Call read-only functions or send transactions for writes and await confirmation.
Representative static code (visual only)
// Create provider and signer
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
await provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []);
const signer = await provider.getSigner();

// Contract instance
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, signer);

// Read
const value = await contract.getData();

// Write
const tx = await contract.setData(500);
await tx.wait();
This static snippet demonstrates the pattern. For the lab, replace the address and ABI with your deployed contract values and test both read and write flows.

screens.title: Reading vs Writing on-chain
screens.subtitle: When operations require gas and signatures vs when they do not

narration.text: A core distinction in DApp development is between read-only operations and state-changing transactions. Reads, such as calling a view or pure function generated for a public state variable, execute locally on a node and do not require a signature or gas. They are fast, free, and often used to display current state in the UI. Writes, on the other hand, modify blockchain state, must be packaged as signed transactions, and require gas to execute. For example, reading getData returns the stored number; invoking setData requires a signed transaction and a gas fee. A common developer trap is assuming reads will reflect immediately after a transaction is sent; they reflect only after the transaction is mined and the state is included in a confirmed block. Another practical consideration is UX: because writes take time and cost money, your UI should clearly tell the user when a transaction is pending, show gas estimates, and display success or failure once confirmed. For debugging, use call-based simulations like callStatic or test networks to verify write logic before using real funds. Closing reflection: how will you design your UI to avoid confusing reads with pending writes and to manage user expectations around cost and confirmation time?

keyIdea.title: Read vs write
keyIdea.text: Reads are free node calls; writes are signed transactions requiring gas and confirmation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Reading vs Writing
Read operations
View or pure functions; executed as node calls; no gas or signature required.
Example
getData() returns a stored number and can be displayed instantly from a node response.
Gotcha
Reads do not require wallet confirmation, so they cannot change state or cost gas.
Write operations
State-changing functions require signed transactions and gas; frontends must request user approval via the wallet.
User experience
Show gas estimates, pending status, and confirmations. Allow cancel or retry where appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Design clear UI states for pending transactions and avoid assuming reads immediately reflect unconfirmed writes.

screens.title: Wallets and Transaction Signing
screens.subtitle: How wallets like MetaMask enable a user to authorize state changes

narration.text: User wallets are central to DApp security and identity. Wallet software securely stores private keys and exposes a signing interface. In a browser context, wallets such as MetaMask inject a provider that allows a DApp to request account access and prompt the user to sign transactions. The flow is consistent: the DApp asks the provider to request accounts; the wallet shows a permission prompt; if the user approves, the provider exposes a signer representing the account. When the DApp requests a state change, the wallet shows transaction details—destination, gas, and estimated fees—so the user can approve or reject. A key benefit of this model is that private keys never leave the user's wallet; signing happens locally. A common misconception is assuming the wallet will automatically sign transactions; in practice, every state-changing call requires explicit user approval. Another important design choice is handling network mismatches: if the DApp is deployed to Sepolia and the wallet is on a different network, transaction attempts will fail. As you build, show clear network and account details to users, and provide friendly errors when signing fails. Finally, consider how events and confirmations are surfaced so the user understands when state is final. How will your UI help users trust the signing process without overwhelming them with technical details?

keyIdea.title: Wallet role
keyIdea.text: Wallets manage private keys, prompt the user for transaction approval, and provide signed transactions to the network.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Wallets & Signing
Why wallets matter
They hold keys, sign transactions, and gate state changes with explicit user consent.
Security model
Private keys remain local; the wallet signs requests after user approval; DApps never receive raw private keys.
User permission
Each write requires the wallet's confirmation dialog and a signature from the user's account.
Practical flow
Detect provider, request eth_requestAccounts, wait for wallet approval, and use the returned signer for transactions. Show gas estimates and pending/confirmed states.
Example
When calling setData, MetaMask displays gas and asks the user to sign; after approval, the network will receive a signed transaction which the DApp can await for mining.
Key Takeaway

Design transparent signing flows and clear network/account indicators so users understand cost and confirmation expectations.

screens.title: Lab Workflow: Connect MetaMask and Interact
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step practical procedure for the demo page

narration.text: This lab follows a reproducible workflow so you can reliably connect a frontend to a deployed AdvancedStorage contract. Step one: prepare your environment by knowing the deployed contract address and ABI, and ensure MetaMask is installed and connected to Sepolia. Step two: open the local index. html demo. The page includes a static code pattern that creates a provider, requests accounts, and obtains a signer. Step three: instantiate the contract object with address and ABI. Step four: Read current state using the view function and display the value in the page. Step five: enter a new number and trigger a state change; MetaMask will prompt you to sign and show gas. Step six: after sending the transaction, wait for confirmation and re-read the contract to display the updated value. A frequent debugging tip is to open the browser console to observe errors, which often reveal mismatched ABI shapes or incorrect addresses. Another tip is to simulate writes with callStatic or run unit tests on a local node before calling mainnet or a public testnet. Reflection: after completing the lab, ask yourself which UI elements reduced friction and which caused confusion for users during signing.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Prepare address/ABI → connect MetaMask → instantiate contract → read value → send transaction → await confirmation and re-read.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Lab Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Confirm your AdvancedStorage contract address and ABI from Remix or your deployment logs.
  2. Open the demo page and detect window.ethereum; create a provider.
  3. Request accounts and get a signer; instantiate the contract with address and ABI.
  4. Call getData to display the current value.
  5. Enter a new value, call setData, approve the MetaMask prompt, and wait for confirmation.
  6. Re-call getData to verify the update and listen for DataChanged events if desired.
Debug checklist
If something fails, check network selection in MetaMask, the contract address, ABI format, and whether the provider supports signing. Use console logs to inspect provider and signer objects.
Quick snippet for verification
// After connect
console.log('Signer address:', await signer.getAddress());
console.log('Contract methods:', Object.keys(contract));
Key Takeaway

Follow the steps and use the console to diagnose network, address, or ABI mismatches quickly.

screens.title: Benefits and Challenges of DApps
screens.subtitle: Why builders choose DApps and where trade-offs appear

narration.text: DApps bring meaningful benefits but also tangible challenges that every developer must weigh. Benefits include censorship resistance: no single operator can unilaterally remove the application; transparency: transactions and contract logic are publicly verifiable; security: cryptographic guarantees protect state against simple tampering; and user ownership: users control their keys and assets. For many use cases these are compelling advantages. However, challenges are significant. Scalability limits and gas fees can make frequent state changes expensive. User experience is another major hurdle: onboarding users to wallets, explaining gas, and handling pending confirmations complicate design. Immutability means bugs are costly—an incorrect contract can be permanent unless you employ upgradeability patterns. Development complexity also increases: testing must include on-chain behaviors, and debugging requires reading logs and events. Regulatory uncertainty adds another dimension; laws around decentralized services may still be evolving. A common misconception is to assume DApps are simply decentralized versions of existing apps; rather, they require rethinking ownership, incentives, and operational models. The takeaway is to design with prudence: place only essential logic and state on-chain, optimize UX around transactions, and plan for testing and upgrade strategies. Which trade-offs in your project will you accept to gain decentralization?

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: DApps offer transparency and user ownership but require careful handling of gas, UX, immutability, and testing complexity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Benefits & Challenges
Benefits
  • Censorship resistance: No single operator can take down the DApp.
  • Transparency: Transactions and logic are auditable on-chain.
  • User ownership: Users control keys and assets directly.
Challenges
  • Scalability & gas: Transactions cost money and take time to confirm.
  • UX complexity: Wallets, gas, and confirmations are friction points.
  • Immutability: Bugs require planned upgrade or migration strategies.
Key Takeaway

Decide what must be on-chain for trust and design UX to manage cost and latency. Plan for upgrades, testing, and clear user communication about gas and confirmations.

narration.text: These compact concept cards recall essential terms you will use as a DApp developer. First, a Decentralized Application runs logic on a blockchain with smart contracts as its backend. Second, a Web3 Provider is the interface that lets a frontend communicate with a node and, frequently, a wallet. Third, libraries like Web3. js and Ethers. js provide convenient APIs to create provider and signer objects, instantiate contract instances, and perform reads and writes. Memorize these terms and be able to explain how they connect: provider bridges frontend to node, signer represents the account that authorizes writes, and the contract enforces rules on-chain. When you work in the lab, refer back to these definitions to reason about failures and design decisions. Can you explain in one sentence how a provider and a signer differ?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Provider, signer, contract and ABI are the vocabulary that describes frontend–blockchain interactions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Key Concepts
Decentralized Application
An app where backend logic and state live on a blockchain.
Web3 Provider
Interface that connects frontend code to a blockchain node.
Ethers.js / Web3.js
Libraries that abstract RPC to let JavaScript interact with contracts.
Summary

These terms are the vocabulary for building DApps: provider, signer, contract, and ABI describe how the frontend communicates with on-chain logic.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Additional terms and a final takeaway

narration.text: Here are a few more compact concepts to lock in your understanding. First, a User Wallet like MetaMask stores keys and prompts signatures for transactions. Second, an ABI describes contract functions and events so external applications can form correct calls. Third, a signer is an object representing a private key capable of signing state-changing transactions within libraries like Ethers. js. Remember the practical interplay: the ABI and address let you instantiate a contract; the provider connects you to a node; the signer authorizes writes via a wallet. These pieces together let your frontend safely and predictably interact with deployed contracts. Final reflection: when you build your DApp, make a checklist of address, ABI, provider URL or wallet, and the target network before attempting any interaction. That checklist will save time when debugging.

keyIdea.title: Final recall
keyIdea.text: Wallets, ABI, and signer are practical elements you must verify before interacting with a deployed contract.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Key Concepts — Part 2
User Wallet
Manages keys, prompts signatures, and injects providers like MetaMask.
ABI
A JSON description of contract functions and events used to build a contract instance.
Signer
Represents an account that can sign transactions for state-changing calls.
Final takeaway

Before running interactions verify: contract address, ABI, provider or wallet, and the active network. A short checklist prevents most common errors.
